correctness.rationale: Under homogeneous K_m-free finite-diagram realization, every one-point named neighborhood is free for parameter clique number <=m-2. For two fresh points, nonadjacent diagrams contribute 4^n; adjacent diagrams only fail if a K_(m-2) lies in the common named neighborhood. In a complete (m-2)-partite base this occurs iff every part contains a common neighbor, with product count of (4^a-3^a) across parts. All smaller part-ranks have no obstruction. The inverse lemma follows rigorously by cancelling largest unmatched size and invoking the primitive prime divisor of 4^d-3^d for each d>=2; singleton parts are recovered from n=log2(t1). The exceptions of Zsigmondy do not apply. Explicit first collisions establish sharpness. The packaged stdlib verifier independently checked 64 finite clique diagrams and 74,481 partition fingerprints; these tests are auxiliary, not claimed an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The novelty target is not Henson homogeneity, the one-point type count, or the classical Bang--Zsigmondy theorem, but the exact critical part-rank obstruction and recovery of all (arbitrarily many) shore sizes from only two numerical tuple-type counts. The closest published formula has m-1 parts in K_m-free graphs, where one-point neighborhoods are constrained and the correction is a sum over missing parts; it does not imply the present product or its primitive-divisor injectivity. A two-shore specialization covers two shores; the present scope m>=5 and k=m-2>=3 requires an unbounded multiset argument. The comparison is statement/implication level; historical exhaustive priority cannot be guaranteed.
residual_risks: There may be an equivalent finite-structure reconstruction theorem under a different terminology or in unindexed historical literature.

value.rationale: The low-arity numerical orbit-spectrum reconstruction problem is natural for homogeneous relational structures. A sharp transition at the parameter clique rank m-2 distinguishes families where pair counts are wholly blind to multipartite structure from those where one additional type count recovers arbitrarily many part sizes. The proof requires genuine prime-divisor rigidity and a nontrivial global inverse argument, not a renamed k=2 calculation or a minor numerical improvement. The n=k+2 first-collision example and effective finite inverse procedure give a motivated sharp boundary; no efficiency or arbitrary-base conclusion is claimed.
